look_here_first: TANGLEHEAD: from the perennial warm-season tuft, inspect its slender, mainly one-sided flowering raceme. Long brown/dark twisted and often bent AWNS from the sessile fertile spikelets can reach roughly 5–8 cm and entwine at maturity. At 10–20× verify one attached fertile SESSILE spikelet and PEDICELLED companion and examine its sharply pointed, hairy CALLUS (often 2–3 mm) beneath the fertile lemma. Early green heads, fully extended dark awns, tangled mature heads and an erect tuft are illustrated separately. Do not identify from yellow grass color alone.

best_field_traits: TANGLEHEAD: native warm-season perennial tuft whose tightly clustered fertile florets bear extraordinarily LONG TWISTED or bent dark awns, which eventually TANGLE together as seedheads mature. Look for the paired sessile and pedicelled spikelets under 10× and the pale hairy raceme around them. A fresh un-tangled head can still be diagnostic from its long awns.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Complete intact rooted flowering tuft and one mature awn-bearing raceme
Measured long bent/twisted dark awn along full length and basal needle-sharp hairy callus at 1-mm resolution
Paired sessile fertile and pedicelled companion spikelets on ONE attached rachis internode under 10–20×
True collar and fringed/ciliate ligule macro and leaflet with scale
Local KR and silver bluestem and little bluestem same-scale field lookalikes
crew_field_check: See green narrow axis, then long dark awns in real photos; do not confuse purple flowering structures with awns
Compare one source-licensed mature intertwined-awn image; note it is nonlocal
Inspect one fertile sessile/pedicelled companion spikelet PAIR under lens and find its sharp hairy basal callus
Avoid identification from straw color or bunch shape alone; historic native metrics untouched

comparisons.key_distinctions: Unlike KR/silver bluestem (Bothriochloa spp.), tanglehead has strikingly long, dark twisting awns from sessile spikelets on narrow racemes; at maturity the awns can intertwine into a spire. Little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium) is recognizable by its fine silvery seed tufts and flowering-branch architecture rather than a concentrated dark tangle. Introduced Dichanthium can have rather fingerlike or branched racemes, with different paired spikelet/glume characters. Confirm under lens, not from posture alone. The sharp hairy callus and sessile + pedicelled companion structure are key unphotographed microcharacters.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Four-stage tanglehead: green head → awn → bunch → tangle
steps: Use photo 1 to see narrow green overlapping spikelet units and pale hairs; visible pinkish exserted structures are not labelled as male or female without secure anatomy.
Photo 2 shows slim racemes bearing very long dark awns; several tips leave the frame, so no awn length is measured.
Photo 3 documents the erect mature tuft, NOT a rooted crown or a flowering microscopic part.
Photo 4 is a separately credited South African mature seedhead: the long awns visibly intertwine. It is not Hays-range evidence.
Confirm one attached fertile sessile spikelet and its pedicelled companion at 10–20×; identify the needle-sharp, beard-hairy basal callus, and measure an individual full dark awn.
Compare KR and silver bluestem and little bluestem seedheads with their actual paired spikelet patterns; color and bunch stature are insufficient.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Distinctive long twisted awns on a fairly narrow raceme, often tangled at maturity, plus attached fertile sessile/pedicelled spikelet pair and sharp hairy basal callus. Silhouette is first-pass, true specimen structure is confirmation.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: 3 original physical image files are source-labelled but not independently vouchered local observations. External mature image is licensed CC BY-SA and explicitly from South Africa; original is not stored in GitHub. Coanne early image is CC BY-NC and MUST remain on noncommercial educational pages with credit. Neither ligule, actual complete measured awn nor sharply pointed callus is shown.
